evidence.claim: Mountain climbs and hundreds of bends give the Dragon its name.
evidence.quote: The Back of the Dragon crosses Big Walker, Brushy and Clinch Mountains along its route that runs from Hungry Mother State Park north of Marion for 32 miles (51 km) to Tazewell. Larry Brent Davidson spearheaded the naming of this section of the road because the route reminded him of the humps on the back of a dragon.

evidence.claim: Mountain climbs and hundreds of bends give the Dragon its name.
evidence.quote: It is a noted route of 32 miles (51 km) that has several hundred sharp turns, scenic overlooks

evidence.claim: Route 16 crosses mountains and valleys between Sugar Grove and Tazewell, passing Hungry Mother Lake north of Marion.
evidence.quote: After a flat area near Sugar Grove, SR 16 again heads uphill, north and northwest across Brushy Mountain and the Appalachian Trail.

evidence.claim: Route 16 crosses mountains and valleys between Sugar Grove and Tazewell, passing Hungry Mother Lake north of Marion.
evidence.quote: The road again heads uphill, passing the west shore of Hungry Mother Lake and the entrance to Hungry Mother State Park

evidence.claim: The 32-mile stretch between Hungry Mother State Park and Tazewell is known as the Back of the Dragon, with hundreds of sharp turns and scenic overlooks.
evidence.quote: It is a noted route of 32 miles (51 km) that has several hundred sharp turns, scenic overlooks

evidence.claim: The 32-mile stretch between Hungry Mother State Park and Tazewell is known as the Back of the Dragon
evidence.quote: The Back of the Dragon crosses Big Walker, Brushy and Clinch Mountains along its route that runs from Hungry Mother State Park north of Marion for 32 miles (51 km) to Tazewell.

evidence.claim: North of Marion, the road winds over Walker Mountain into Rich Valley and crosses the North Fork Holston River at Chatham Hill before climbing again.
evidence.quote: SR 16 crosses Walker Mountain in a curving route, coming down into the Rich Valley and crossing the North Fork Holston River at Chatham Hill

evidence.claim: Larry Brent Davidson led the effort to name it: the succession of mountain crossings reminded him of a dragon’s back.
evidence.quote: Larry Brent Davidson spearheaded the naming of this section of the road because the route reminded him of the humps on the back of a dragon.

evidence.claim: The highway took shape in pieces. In 1928, the state added road sections extending north and south from Marion as Route 113.
evidence.quote: In 1928, the next piece of SR 16, running north and south from State Route 10 (now U.S. Route 11 in Marion, 6.8 miles (10.9 km) in each direction, was added to the state highway system as State Route 113.

evidence.claim: In 1933, the Route 113 sections through Marion and south from Tazewell became Route 88.
evidence.quote: Both pieces of SR 113 - through Marion and south from Tazewell - became State Route 88 in the 1933 renumbering.

evidence.claim: The remaining gap in Tazewell County was filled in 1937 and 1938.
evidence.quote: the gap in Tazewell County was filled in 1937 and 1938.

evidence.claim: The 1940 renumbering assembled the present Route 16 from several earlier numbered roads.
evidence.quote: In the 1940 renumbering, the present route of State Route 16 was assigned over all of SR 92 and SR 88 and the part of SR 81 north of Tazewell.

evidence.claim: Driving south from Tazewell, pass through Thompson Valley before the hairpin climb toward Clinch Mountain.
evidence.quote: This time, a single hairpin turn takes it into the wide Thompson Valley, where it passes the community of Thompson Valley.

evidence.claim: Continue across Freestone Valley and Brushy Mountain, then through Rich Valley and over Walker Mountain to Hungry Mother Lake and Marion.
evidence.quote: Another twisty descent takes SR 16 down Brushy Mountain into the Freestone Valley, but almost immediately it must rise again to cross Clinch Mountain.

evidence.claim: Continue across Freestone Valley and Brushy Mountain, then through Rich Valley and over Walker Mountain to Hungry Mother Lake and Marion.
evidence.quote: SR 16 crosses Walker Mountain in a curving route, coming down into the Rich Valley and crossing the North Fork Holston River at Chatham Hill and State Route 42 soon after at Black Hill. Again SR 16 heads uphill, climbing Brushy Mountain to the county line.

evidence.claim: Beyond Marion, Route 16 follows Staley Creek, crosses the Appalachian Trail and Brushy Mountain, and descends toward Sugar Grove.
evidence.quote: After a flat area near Sugar Grove, SR 16 again heads uphill, north and northwest across Brushy Mountain and the Appalachian Trail. It then runs northwest, following Staley Creek downhill past Attoway and Furnace Hill and through several gaps into Marion.

evidence.claim: A five-cent streetcar once connected North Tazewell’s station and industrial complexes with downtown Main Street.
evidence.quote: Chartered as the Tazewell Railway and Light Company, it operated from Tazewell station and industrial complexes in North Tazewell to downtown along Main Street

evidence.claim: A five-cent streetcar
evidence.quote: The fare was five cents.

evidence.claim: The Tazewell Railway and Light Company began with horse-drawn cars in 1892 and electrified the line in 1904.
evidence.quote: The trolley started operations in 1892 as a horsecar and it was electrified in 1904.

evidence.claim: By 1920, it faced competition from automobiles; service ended in 1933.
evidence.quote: By 1920, the streetcar was competing with automobiles and it closed in 1933.

evidence.claim: Route 16 now runs through downtown on Main Street and Fincastle Turnpike.
evidence.quote: The overlapped routes pass through downtown Tazewell on Main Street and Fincastle Turnpike

evidence.claim: The courthouse dates from 1874 but was rebuilt in Classical Revival style in 1913, during the trolley era.
evidence.quote: The most notable building is the Tazewell County Courthouse.  It was built in 1874, and rebuilt in 1913 in a Classical Revival style.

evidence.claim: The town itself changed names in 1892, the year the horsecar began running: before then, it had been called Jeffersonville.
evidence.quote: Named Jeffersonville until 1892, Tazewell developed near the headwaters of the Clinch River.

evidence.claim: Thompson Valley is a wide interval between mountain crossings on Route 16.
evidence.quote: This time, a single hairpin turn takes it into the wide Thompson Valley

evidence.claim: Traveling south, the highway leaves the valley through a hairpin on the way up Clinch Mountain, then drops into Freestone Valley before climbing Brushy Mountain.
evidence.quote: Another twisty descent takes SR 16 down Brushy Mountain into the Freestone Valley, but almost immediately it must rise again to cross Clinch Mountain. This time, a single hairpin turn takes it into the wide Thompson Valley

evidence.claim: The community takes its name from William and Archibald Thompson, who settled it in the early 19th century.
evidence.quote: It is named after William and Archibald Thompson, who first settled the community in the early 19th century.

evidence.claim: Route 16 passes the west shore of Hungry Mother Lake and the entrance to its state park.
evidence.quote: passing the west shore of Hungry Mother Lake and the entrance to Hungry Mother State Park

evidence.claim: The 108-acre lake and sandy beach are the park’s principal features.
evidence.quote: The park's main feature is a 108-acre lake with a sandy beach.

evidence.claim: Local landowners donated much of the land, and the Civilian Conservation Corps built the original grounds, trails and campsites.
evidence.quote: Much of the land for Hungry Mother State Park was donated by local landowners to develop a new state park in Smyth County on Hungry Mother Creek. The original grounds, trails and campsites of the park were built CCC

evidence.claim: Hungry Mother opened on June 15, 1936, with five other Virginia state parks. Governor George C. Peery attended the opening here.
evidence.quote: like the other five Virginia state parks that opened on 15 June 1936. Governor George C. Peery attended the opening ceremonies on June 15 at Hungry Mother

evidence.claim: In his opening remarks, Peery linked the park system to Depression-era jobs and recreation for working families.
evidence.quote: remarked that the state park system was something good that came out of the Great Depression, and not only provided CCC jobs for those who lost them in that crisis and needed recreation space for working families

evidence.claim: At its opening, the park admitted white visitors only.
evidence.quote: the initial opening ceremony for the six new state parks at (then whites-only) Hungry Mother State Park

evidence.claim: A sandy beach borders the park’s 108-acre lake.
evidence.quote: The park's main feature is a 108-acre lake with a sandy beach.

flags: Cached List of Virginia Byways has no route table. It cannot verify this road’s Virginia Byway designation, January 20, 2000 date, Dickey Gap–Pisgah extent or a designation-body rationale. Those claims are omitted pending a readable record.

Material strip miles run south from Tazewell through Thompson Valley; moments follow that order. Overview extends south through Marion to Sugar Grove to honor the catalog corridor, without asserting unsupported designation boundaries.
Exact turn count varies from 260 to 438 in cache; used hundreds. No whole-drive time supported.
Thompson Valley moment is short because the local source is only two sentences; route geometry supplies the useful additional context.

Hungry Mother legend is sourced only to an unattributed account with generic Native American identification. Replaced it with documented park construction and opening, including the initial racial exclusion.
Dropped current claim of designated Dickey Gap–Pisgah endpoints because cache omits the supporting table. Omitted speed advice and the hedged smallest-streetcar-town comparison.
